# BERKSHIRE HATHAWAY INC — FUND PORTFOLIO REPORT
### 13F-HR for the period ended June 30, 2026 (filed August 14, 2026)

---

## SNAPSHOT

Berkshire Hathaway Inc. (SEC CIK 0001067983) reported a 13F equity portfolio valued at **$299.25 billion across 29 distinct positions** for the quarter ended **June 30, 2026**, filed **August 14, 2026** [3][5][7]. The cover page lists **89 entries and 14 other included managers**, and indicates **no confidential treatment** was requested — meaning the disclosed set appears complete as filed, with no positions withheld from public view. The prior filing period was **March 31, 2026**.

The reported value rose **13.74%** from the prior quarter's **$263.10 billion** [3]. That increase reflects both market appreciation and genuine net buying: press coverage of the filing describes Berkshire as a **net buyer of roughly $19.8 billion** in publicly traded equities during the quarter, **ending a 14-quarter selling streak** [4], with the company's own Q2 earnings report showing approximately **$23.5 billion in marketable equity purchases** [8][10]. This is Greg Abel's first year as chief executive, and the shift from seller to buyer is the single most important context for reading this filing [10].

**Essential caveats.** A Form 13F-HR discloses only **long U.S.-listed equity and equity-option positions**. It **excludes short positions, cash and Treasury bills, non-U.S.-listed holdings, and most fixed income**, and it is filed **up to 45 days after quarter-end** — so this is a **lagged snapshot as of June 30, 2026**, not a real-time or complete picture of Berkshire's book. This distinction matters unusually much here: Berkshire holds an enormous cash and Treasury position and large non-U.S. equity stakes (web reporting notes purchases of the Japanese trading houses Mitsubishi, Marubeni and Sumitomo disclosed earlier in the quarter), none of which appear in the $299.25 billion figure. Berkshire is also an operating conglomerate whose wholly owned businesses — and reported acquisitions such as Taylor Morrison — sit entirely outside the 13F.

---

## TOP HOLDINGS

The book remains extraordinarily concentrated. Per the latest 13F, the top five positions are:

| # | Holding | Value | % of portfolio | Shares |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Apple Inc | $65.95B | 22.0% | 227,917,808 |
| 2 | American Express Co | $51.28B | 17.1% | 151,610,700 |
| 3 | Coca-Cola Co | $32.51B | 10.9% | 400,000,000 |
| 4 | Alphabet Inc (Class A) | $28.16B | 9.4% | 78,791,167 |
| 5 | Bank of America Corp | $27.54B | 9.2% | 483,394,015 |

Those five account for **76.5%** of reported value [4], and the top ten reach a **top-10 concentration of 88.5%** [5]. Rounding out the top ten: Chevron ($13.99B, 4.7%), Occidental Petroleum ($12.87B, 4.3%), Chubb ($11.67B, 3.9%), Moody's ($11.17B, 3.7%) and the second Alphabet line — Class C — at $9.61B (3.2%).

Because Alphabet is reported on two lines, the economic exposure is understated by the ranking. Combining the Class A and Class C stakes gives roughly **$37.76 billion, about 12.62% of the 13F portfolio**, which makes Alphabet Berkshire's **third-largest marketable equity investment** ahead of Coca-Cola on a combined basis [4].

Below the top ten, the tail is small but recognizable: Kraft Heinz ($7.69B, 2.6%), DaVita ($6.43B, 2.1%), Delta Air Lines ($5.37B, 1.8%), SiriusXM ($3.69B, 1.2%) and VeriSign ($2.26B, 0.8%). With 29 positions and 88.5% of value in ten names [5], this is a high-conviction book in which anything outside the top ten is effectively a rounding item — and reported quarterly turnover was just **1.5%** [5].

---

## PORTFOLIO CHANGES

The material provided lists **1 new position, 7 additions, 6 reductions and 1 exit** versus the March 31, 2026 filing [5], with the largest rows in each bucket shown below.

**New position (1 of 1 listed):**
- **D.R. Horton Inc — $581K.** A token starter stake; web reporting puts it at **3,564 shares, ~$580,000**, and links it to Berkshire's broader homebuilding tilt alongside the acquisition of Taylor Morrison [9].

**Added to (7 total; all shown):**
- **Alphabet Inc (Class A): +24,541,369 shares, +45.2%** from 54,249,798 shares (~$8.77B at quarter-end value)
- **Alphabet Inc (Class C): +23,603,218 shares, +658.3%** from 3,585,215 shares (~$8.34B)
- **Delta Air Lines: +17,510,544 shares, +44.0%** from 39,809,456 shares (~$1.64B)
- **Lennar Corp (Class A): +3,012,099 shares, +29.8%** from 10,099,642 shares (~$272.6M)
- **Macy's Inc: +4,309,071 shares, +141.8%** from 3,038,355 shares (~$101.5M)
- **New York Times Co: +553,465 shares, +3.7%** from 15,146,535 shares (~$38.7M)
- **Lennar Corp (Class B): +60,414 shares, +25.4%** from 237,703 shares (~$5.4M)

Web reporting attributes the Alphabet build to a **$10 billion private placement in June plus an additional $5–7 billion of open-market stock purchased through the quarter** [4] — an important detail, because the private-placement component means the increase was not purely a market-based accumulation.

**Trimmed (6 total; all shown):**
- **Bank of America: −30,230,150 shares, −5.9%** of a prior 513,624,165 shares (~$1.72B)
- **Capital One Financial: −4,150,000 shares, −58.0%** of 7,150,000 shares (~$832.6M)
- **Kroger: −11,000,000 shares, −22.0%** of 50,000,000 shares (~$610.8M)
- **Nucor: −2,049,323 shares, −52.5%** of 3,907,075 shares (~$456.5M)
- **DaVita: −1,220,376 shares, −4.1%** of 30,100,585 shares (~$271.5M)
- **Ally Financial: −2,000,000 shares, −6.9%** of 29,000,000 shares (~$91.9M)

**Exited (1 of 1 listed):** **Constellation Brands**, previously 632,890 shares [7].

Equally telling is what did *not* move. The three largest positions — Apple, American Express and Coca-Cola, together **50.0%** of the portfolio — were left **unchanged in share count** [3]. The entire quarter's activity happened around a static core.

---

## NOTABLE MOVES & WHAT THEY SIGNAL

**1. Alphabet is the statement trade.** Adding roughly **$17 billion of combined Class A and Class C exposure** in one quarter — including a 658% increase in the Class C line off a small base — took Alphabet from a peripheral holding to roughly 12.6% of the 13F book [4]. This is not a nibble; it is a top-three commitment made in a single quarter, and web coverage attributes the decision to Warren Buffett personally [4]. The use of a **private placement** [4] suggests the size sought exceeded what could be accumulated quietly in the open market.

**2. The selling streak is over.** Ending **14 consecutive quarters** of net selling [4][10] with roughly **$19.8–23.5 billion** deployed [4][8] is a regime change in behaviour, not a tactical tweak. The 13F cannot show the cash side of that ledger, but the direction of travel is unambiguous.

**3. A deliberate housing tilt.** Lennar Class A (+29.8%), Lennar Class B (+25.4%) and the new D.R. Horton stake — reinforced outside the 13F by the Taylor Morrison acquisition [9] — form a coherent, if small, thematic bet on U.S. homebuilding. The dollar amounts are trivial relative to portfolio size (~$278M of Lennar adds, ~$581K of D.R. Horton), so read this as an option on a theme, not a core allocation.

**4. Banks: selective retreat, not wholesale exit.** Bank of America was cut a further 5.9% — described in coverage as a **consecutive quarter of trimming** [12] — while **Capital One was halved (−58.0%)** and Ally cut 6.9%. Yet Bank of America still stands at $27.54B and 9.2% of the book. The pattern is pruning smaller and more consumer-credit-levered financials while keeping the flagship bank stake large but shrinking. American Express, untouched, remains the preferred financial exposure at 17.1%.

**5. Recycling out of low-conviction tails.** Nucor (−52.5%), Kroger (−22.0%), the Constellation Brands exit, and small DaVita trimming read as housekeeping — coverage characterises it as "cleaning up smaller legacy positions" [11] — freeing capital for the Alphabet and Delta adds.

**6. Delta's 44% increase** (to 57,320,000 shares, $5.37B) is a notable re-embrace of an airline, a sector Berkshire had historically exited, and the second-largest dollar add of the quarter.

---

## CLOSING READ

This filing captures a genuine inflection: a stable, hyper-concentrated core (Apple, American Express, Coca-Cola untouched at half the portfolio) surrounded by the most decisive capital deployment in three years [10]. The character of the new money is instructive — a mega-cap technology platform bought at scale, plus smaller, cyclical, domestically levered bets in homebuilding, airlines and even Macy's — funded partly by halving positions in second-tier financials and industrials. Turnover of just 1.5% [5] confirms this was surgical rather than a rebuild.

Two limits on interpretation deserve emphasis. First, the 13F is **long U.S.-listed equity only** and was filed six weeks after the period end; Berkshire's cash, Treasuries, Japanese trading-house stakes and wholly owned operating businesses are all invisible here, so this is a **partial and lagged view** of a much larger balance sheet. Second, only the largest rows of each change bucket are reproduced above — the material provided here lists one new position, seven adds, six trims and one exit, and readers should not infer that nothing else occurred beyond the itemised lines.
